title: Check yourself: text blocks in use

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A product listing builds `SELECT ... ORDER BY %s` from a text block with `formatted(sort)`, where `sort` comes from the URL. To close the injection a tester found there, a developer changes the block to end in `ORDER BY ?` and calls `ps.setString(1, sort)` on the `PreparedStatement`. What does the change achieve?

options.text: The URL can no longer change the statement, and the listing now sorts by the column it names, since the driver sends that name apart from the statement text
options.says: a placeholder stands only for a value; a column in ORDER BY can't be bound

options.text: The URL can no longer change the statement, and the listing no longer sorts by the column it names, since what is bound there is a value and not a column
options.says: the bound text stays a value, so it can't inject, and for the same reason it isn't a column name; identifiers come from a fixed set

options.text: The URL can still change the statement, since setString copies the text into the statement just as formatted did
options.says: with a placeholder the statement text stays the same constant and the value travels separately through setString

options.text: The URL can still change the statement, since a placeholder after ORDER BY is filled in before the statement is parsed
options.says: the statement text sent to prepareStatement is the same for every input; the value is sent apart from it

origin.section: A Value Formatted Into SQL Becomes SQL; a Bind Parameter Stays a Value

questions.stem: A test reads `expected/summary.txt` with `Files.readString` and compares it with `isEqualTo` to a report the code builds from a text block. It passes on the Linux build agents. On the Windows agent, which checks the repository out with `core.autocrlf=true`, it fails, and the failure message shows the same lines on both sides. What differs?

options.text: The line endings, since the checked-out file ends its lines with \r\n and the text block ends them with \n
options.says: a text block's lines end with \n on every platform; the checkout converted the file's to \r\n

options.text: The line endings, since the text block ends its lines with \r\n on Windows and the checked-out file ends them with \n
options.says: a text block's line terminators are \n whatever the platform

options.text: The final newline, since the checked-out file loses its final line break and the text block keeps one
options.says: the file read back still ends with its line break, now \r\n

options.text: The final newline, since the text block drops its final line break on Windows and the checked-out file keeps one
options.says: the final newline depends on where the closing delimiter sits, not on the platform

origin.section: A Text Block Fixture Has `\n` Line Endings, So Compare Lines When the Format Doesn't Care

questions.stem: A label scanner keeps its tracking-number regex in a static final text block, one part per line with a `# ...` note after each part, and compiles it with `Pattern.compile(TRACKING)` and no flags. It is given a label that holds a valid tracking number. What does `find()` return?

options.text: It returns true, since javac removes the line breaks, the spaces and the notes before the regex engine sees them
options.says: javac removes only incidental indentation; the line breaks, the remaining spaces and the notes stay in the string, so the engine must match them

options.text: It returns false, since the line breaks, the spaces and the notes are characters the engine must find in the label
options.says: without comments mode the layout is part of the pattern, and the match fails without an error

options.text: It throws PatternSyntaxException, since the notes start with a #, which is a syntax error outside comments mode
options.says: outside comments mode # is an ordinary character to match; the pattern compiles and simply fails to match

options.text: It throws PatternSyntaxException, since parts and notes on several lines need the MULTILINE flag
options.says: the pattern compiles; the line breaks are characters it must match, which is why it finds nothing

origin.section: A Regex in a Text Block Keeps Its Line Breaks, So It Needs Comments Mode

questions.stem: A validator compiles this text block as its pattern, with no flags passed: the first line is `(?x)` and the second is `^ Invoice \\d+ $    # invoice number`. Which of the inputs `Invoice 77` and `Invoice77` does `find()` accept?

options.text: Only `Invoice 77`, since the space between the word and the number is matched as it is written
options.says: in comments mode white space in the pattern is ignored, so the written space matches nothing

options.text: Only `Invoice77`, since white space in the pattern is ignored in this mode
options.says: (?x) ignores the pattern's spaces; a space meant to match is written \\x20, or \\s for any white space

options.text: Both of them, since (?x) makes white space in the input optional
options.says: comments mode changes how the pattern is read, not the input; the space in the input has nothing to match it

options.text: Neither of them, since the line break after (?x) is part of the pattern to match
options.says: in comments mode the line break is white space and is ignored like the spaces

origin.section: A Regex in a Text Block Keeps Its Line Breaks, So It Needs Comments Mode

concepts: In comments mode a space written in the pattern is ignored, so a space to be matched is written as \\s or [ ].
A placeholder stands only for a value: binding a column name after ORDER BY closes the injection but doesn't sort by that column.
A regex laid out over the lines of a text block matches its line breaks, spaces and notes literally unless it is compiled in comments mode.
A text block's lines end with \n on every platform, while a file checked out with core.autocrlf=true ends them with \r\n.
